Use this page to extract the dates a time-to-event analysis needs: the date of
the first outcome event after index, and the dates of death and emigration that
end follow-up. It builds on [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd), which
explains the diagnosis extraction and defines the helper used below. You finish
with one small `.rds` file per date (`pnr` plus one date column), ready to be
linked onto the cohort in [Phase 12](data-manipulation.qmd).

<details>
<summary>Why you need death and emigration dates as well as the outcome</summary>

In a time-to-event study you follow each person from the index date until the outcome occurs, or until the outcome can no longer be observed. A person who dies or emigrates disappears from the Danish registers, and you cannot know whether they later developed the outcome. So you censor them on the death or emigration date. Follow-up then ends at the earliest of outcome, death, emigration and end of study.

If a competing event (for example death) precludes your outcome rather than just ending follow-up, it is a competing risk. That is handled in the analysis, see [Competing risks](time-to-event.qmd#competing-risks).

</details>

## Extract the first outcome event after index {#the-pattern}

The outcome is typically the first hospital diagnosis after index, taken from
LPR (Landspatientregisteret, the Danish National Patient Register).
`read_register()`
requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers, see [Parquet and
fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet) if you did not convert
them from SAS yourself.

```r
library(fastreg) # read_register(), used inside get_lpr_diagnoses()
library(dplyr) # %>%, inner_join(), filter(), slice()

cohort <- readRDS("path/to/full_cohort.rds") # your cohort from Phase 10: pnr + index_date
CODES <- c("S72") # hip fracture (example study) - change to your outcome

# Example: first hip fracture diagnosis after index (outcome)
# lpr_diag has no pnr - pnr and contact date live in lpr_adm (join key recnum).
# get_lpr_diagnoses() from Extract from LPR does that join for LPR2 and LPR3
# and keeps ONLY your cohort; define it first (see Phase 9).
outcome <- get_lpr_diagnoses(unique(cohort$pnr), icd_codes = CODES) %>%
  inner_join(cohort %>% select(pnr, index_date), by = "pnr") %>%
  filter(date_contact > index_date) %>% # AFTER index only = outcome
  group_by(pnr) %>%
  arrange(date_contact) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup() %>% # keep only first event per person
  select(pnr, event_date = date_contact)

saveRDS(outcome, "path/to/extract_hip_fracture.rds") # read again in Phase 12 (Link your extracts)
```

`group_by(pnr)`, `arrange()` and `slice(1)` keep only the first event per
person, which is what most outcome definitions need. The pattern is explained
in [Long ↔ wide format](long-wide.qmd).

The join inside `get_lpr_diagnoses()` assembles one extract: it puts LPR's
contact and diagnosis tables together so that `pnr`, date and diagnosis sit in
one table. Linking the finished extract onto your cohort is a separate step
that comes later, in [Link your extracts](joins.qmd), once all your extractions
are done.

## Death and emigration dates for censoring {#censoring-dates}

Extract the date of death from DOD (the register of deaths, column `doddato`)
and emigrations from VNDS (the migration register, rows with
`indud_kode == "U"`), each as its own table filtered to the cohort. The worked
code for both, including keeping only the first emigration after index, is in
[Link your extracts](joins.qmd); the column names are in [Overview of
registers](register-reference.qmd). Follow-up time is then calculated from the
outcome, death and emigration dates in [Calculate follow-up time and event
variable](joins.qmd#follow-up-time).

## Misclassification: a diagnosis code is a proxy {#misclassification}

::: {.callout-warning}
A register diagnosis is a proxy for the real condition, with its own validity
(sensitivity and positive predictive value, PPV). How wrong it is shapes your
result:

- **Non-differential misclassification:** errors unrelated to exposure (the same
  code validity in both groups) usually bias the effect toward the null, so a
  real effect looks weaker than it is.
- **Differential misclassification:** the outcome is captured more completely in
  one group (for example, exposed people are in contact with the health system
  more often and so get diagnosed more). This can bias the estimate in either
  direction.
:::

What you can do about it: use validated code definitions where they exist, look
up the PPV of your codes, and run a sensitivity analysis with a stricter or
looser definition. For the validity of LPR diagnoses, start with the review by
[Schmidt et al. 2015, *Clinical
Epidemiology*](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S91125) (the Danish National
Patient Registry). Background on measurement bias: [Hernán & Robins, *What If*,
chapter 9](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook).

## Where does your codelist come from? {#where-does-your-codelist-come-from}

Applying a codelist (regex, `%in%`) is the easy part. Deciding which codes make
up your condition is the hard part. Use a published, ideally validated list
where one exists, and document and share your own so others can reproduce it.

- **ICD-10:** for example
  [mltc-codelists](https://github.com/rprigge-uoe/mltc-codelists), ICD-10
  codelists for many chronic conditions, with the accompanying methods paper
  ([Prigge et al. 2025, *Communications
  Medicine*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43856-025-00995-4)).
- **ATC (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical codes, for medication):** define drug
  groups from the [WHO ATC/DDD index](https://atcddd.fhi.no/atc_ddd_index/) and
  published drug-class definitions. See [Medication (ATC)](medication.qmd).
